newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian mini-budget seen as yet another stopgap.
newsitem.headline: Italian mini-budget seen as yet another stopgap.

text.p: A sneak preview of Italy's 1997 mini-budget, expected to be unveiled fully on Thursday, failed to impress economists who said the measures looked set to be the temporary stopgap they had predicted.

Comments from politicians on Wednesday indicated the package will, as expected, be for 15-16 trillion lire ($8.9-9.5 billion) of budget deficit cuts but without the structural changes to state spending which economists say are key to sustained control of Italian accounts.

Hard-left Communist Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti said after meeting Prime Minister Romano Prodi that a third of the money would come from advance tax on company severance payments, a third from spending cuts in some state funds and the rest from new methods of levying certain unspecified taxes.

Ken Wattret, economist at Paribas, said: "It looks like it's going to be the usual mishmash of one-offs and gap-fillers to bring the deficit down. The government is making enormous efforts but the problem is they're not making structural changes."

Italy is striving to meet tough economic criteria to join Europe economic and monetary union (EMU) at its 1999 start and unveiled a huge 62.5 trillion lire budget at the end of last year in a bid to meet the terms of the Maastricht Treaty.
But a 1997 budget deficit which is 3.0 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) is proving a tough EMU target for a country whose 1996 deficit to GDP ratio was 6.7 percent.
Moreover this economic fitness must carry on into 1998.
Analysts said Italy, in taking only short term measures, was not tackling the problem of sustaining EMU goals by failing to act now in areas like reforming the state pension system.

Giovanna Mossetti, chief economist at Milan brokers Caboto, told Reuters Financial Television: "Not only are these one-off measures, these are one-off measures that will come back with a vengeance next year...they are trying to sweep the problem under the carpet."

But the apparent accord between the government and the hard-left, whose support is crucial to Prodi in the lower house of parliament, means some political uncertainty has drained from the financial markets for now, bond brokers said.

This accord implies a compromise to make structural reforms at a later date, they said, although Lorenzo Stanca, economist at Credito Italiano, told RFTV he was not greatly optimistic effective pension reforms would be worked out this year.
On the financial markets, Italian government bonds (Btps) ended little changed on Tuesday's levels and debt futures closed slightly up, although brokers said the market was volatile.

Btp futures brokers in London expressed disappointment the additional budget package looked set to be at most 16 trillion lire, rather than a heftier figure like 20 trillion as had been rumoured in the marketplace earlier on Wednesday.

Brokers in Italy were more positive and pointed out that the lira climbed beyond the psychological 1,000 per mark barrier to 996 lire during Wednesday, although London brokers argued this was as much a technical move on the strength of the dollar than any obvious enthusiasm for the budget.
